clue.text: Corrupt in double time, seemingly?

blocks.note: surface reading: thoroughly crooked, depraved all the way through
setter's reading: the six-letter word for corrupt has two Ts, time twice over, sitting at its very centre

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a thing is corrupted when played at double speed.
explanation.walkthrough: ROTTEN means corrupt, and its middle letters are TT, a doubled T for time, so the time really is at the core of ROTTEN: ROTTEN TO THE CORE.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a person or institution that is wholly and irredeemably bad, every part spoiled.

clue.text: Grating fifth of cheese, sharp object

indicators.note: a fifth of a word here means its fifth letter, not a fraction of its length

blocks.note: the fifth letter of cheese
a three-pronged spear, as carried by Neptune

explanation.surface: A cheese grater taking a fifth off a block is compared to a sharp object.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grating' looks like the cheese grater at work, but it is the adjective meaning harsh-sounding.
explanation.definitionFit: A strident voice is loud and harsh, unpleasant to hear, which is what grating describes.

clue.text: Butcher, a geezer

blocks.note: to fell is to cut down or strike down, as a butcher does
taken as written

explanation.surface: A butcher is described as just some bloke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butcher' reads as a noun naming the man, but it is a verb, meaning to slaughter. A geezer is British slang for a man.
explanation.definitionFit: Fella is an informal spelling of fellow, a casual word for a man, just like geezer.

clue.text: Ground slippery, suddenly sprang back

blocks.note: a rec is a recreation ground, the local playing field
a surface that has been oiled is slippery

explanation.surface: Someone stepping onto slick earth jumps back in alarm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like an anagram signal or the earth underfoot; it is a REC, British shorthand for a public recreation ground.
explanation.definitionFit: To recoil is to spring or flinch backwards, as a gun does on firing or a person in shock.

clue.text: Sweet cuddle when knelt before Spooner?

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so his version of the phrase is wanted

blocks.note: kneeling down, a cuddle would wrap round someone's bottom; swap the opening sounds of that two-word phrase

explanation.surface: A person kneels before the Reverend Spooner for a sweet embrace.
explanation.walkthrough: A humbug is a striped boiled mint sweet popular in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A humbug is a hard peppermint confection, a classic British sweet, which is what Americans call candy.

clue.text: Standard enclosures second

blocks.note: yards are fenced enclosures, as in a stockyard
a tick is a moment, as in 'just a tick'

explanation.surface: Pens of a regulation size come second in a ranking.
explanation.definitionFit: A yardstick is a measure by which things are judged, a benchmark or criterion.

clue.text: Reportedly more than one cheese in piece of cake?

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said or heard, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

blocks.note: plural of brie, the soft French cheese

explanation.surface: Several cheeses are said to be baked into a slice of cake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece of cake' tempts a reading about food alongside the cheese, but it is the idiom for something easy.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeze, like a piece of cake, is an informal word for a task that is very easy to do.

clue.text: Rock nihilists' spat, a nadir for group in film

indicators.note: to rock is to shake or sway, so the letters are jolted into a new order
the nadir is the lowest point, and in a down entry the lowest point of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
taken as written
the bottom letter of group

explanation.surface: A quarrel among nihilist rockers marks the band's low point in a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like the plot of the film itself, a band's disastrous decline. 'Nadir' takes the final letter because in a down clue the end of a word sits lowest.
explanation.definitionFit: This Is Spinal Tap is the 1984 mockumentary film about a hapless heavy metal band.

clue.text: Subject described by improper noun, an option to consume?

indicators.note: something improper is not in its correct form, so the letters are disordered
to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one piece is circled by the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a theme is the subject of a talk or essay

explanation.surface: A grammar note: a subject expressed by an improper noun is something one could take up.
explanation.walkthrough: The grammar terms subject and noun lead toward parts of speech, but the rearranged noun simply splits to wrap round the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: A dish that is on the menu is available to be ordered and eaten, one of the choices offered.

clue.text: As aging rocker, grossly hirsute originally, I'm tearing my hair out!

indicators.note: originally points to how each word begins, so only the opening letters count

blocks.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: An aging, very hairy rocker despairs over losing it.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition fits the surface neatly: the hairy rocker is the one tearing his hair out.
explanation.definitionFit: Aargh is the cry of frustration or exasperation someone gives when they are at their wits' end.

clue.text: Brace having held one log that's loose, shelter built in the woods

indicators.note: to have held something is to have it inside your grip, so one piece is placed within another
something loose is not fixed in place, so these letters may shift around

blocks.note: a brace is a pair, as of game birds
Roman numeral one
the three letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone braces a loose log to build a woodland shelter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brace' looks like a verb about propping the log; it is a noun meaning a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A twigloo is a dome-shaped den made of twigs and branches, a play on igloo, built for camping or forest play.

clue.text: Wrong content in parcels, send a batch back

indicators.note: content means what is held inside, so the letters sit within the following words
back says the hidden letters are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the letters running across the end of parcels, through send and a, into the start of batch

explanation.surface: Someone finds the wrong goods inside packages and returns a whole consignment.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading from the B of batch leftward gives BADNESS.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, wrong is evil or wickedness, the quality of being morally bad.

clue.text: With that, odd number is even for the present time

blocks.clueFragment: With that, odd number is even
blocks.note: surface reading: some arithmetic trick that turns an odd number into an even one
setter's reading: take the first two letters off the odd number eleven and what remains spells even, so the instruction is a phrase meaning 'without EL'

explanation.surface: A maths puzzle claims a certain step makes an odd number even.
explanation.walkthrough: ELEVEN with no EL is EVEN, so the instruction reads NO EL, which is NOEL, Christmas, the time for presents.
explanation.definitionFit: Noel is Christmas, the festive season when gifts are given, so a time of presents.

clue.text: First of fruit dark, like a kiwi, say?

indicators.note: first of points to the opening letter of the word that follows

blocks.note: the initial letter of fruit
without light, so dark

explanation.surface: A kiwi fruit's first part is dark.
explanation.walkthrough: With fruit in the clue, kiwi suggests the fruit; it is the New Zealand bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The kiwi is a bird that cannot fly, and flightless describes such birds; 'say' marks it as one example.

clue.text: Purpose of megaphone, dammit!

blocks.note: first meaning, taken literally: a megaphone is for shouting at volume
second meaning: an exclamation of exasperation

explanation.surface: Someone frustrated asks what on earth a megaphone is for.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a common exclamation of irritation, a milder alternative to swearing, and literally describes amplified shouting.

clue.text: See 15 Down
A bluebottle stuck in prune drink

indicators.note: stuck in means pushed inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: taken as written
to lop is to prune or cut off branches
bluebottle is old slang for a police officer, from the blue uniform

explanation.surface: A fly is found trapped in a prune-flavoured drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bluebottle' paints a fly; it is the dated British slang for a policeman. 'Prune' looks like the dried plum, but it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: An alcopop is a sweet, fruit-flavoured alcoholic beverage sold ready-mixed, like an alcoholic soft drink.

clue.text: Anomalous, a bug fed endless fruit

indicators.note: something fed has food put inside it, so the following piece goes inside the earlier ones
endless means without its end, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
an ant is an insect, loosely a bug
a berry is a small fruit; it loses its last letter

explanation.surface: An odd case: an insect eating fruit with its ends nibbled off.
explanation.walkthrough: The trimmed fruit goes between the A and the ANT, as if fed into the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Aberrant means departing from the normal or expected course, which is what anomalous describes.

clue.text: See 23
Someone choosing anagram of 'Chile' in flier?

indicators.note: the setter names the device outright, asking for the quoted word's letters rearranged

blocks.note: the five letters of the country rearranged
one who opts, a chooser

explanation.surface: Someone picks an anagram of Chile on a printed flyer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flier' looks like a leaflet; it is anything that flies. The two parts appear in the answer in reverse clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: A helicopter is a rotor-driven aircraft, so something that flies; the question mark flags the loose definition.

clue.text: Discontented alligator prodding cat in some box?

indicators.note: without its contents, only the outside letters of the word stay
to prod is to poke into something, so one piece is pushed inside another

blocks.note: the lynx is a wild cat
the first and last letters of alligator

explanation.surface: A sulky alligator pokes a cat that is shut in a box.
explanation.walkthrough: The larynx is the voice box, so 'some box' with a question mark points to it as one kind of box.
explanation.definitionFit: The larynx is the organ in the throat housing the vocal cords, popularly called the voice box.

clue.text: Models, just over three turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: pi is 3.14..., a little more than three
spun means turned round

explanation.surface: Three models were just about to turn up at a show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned up' reads as a phrase meaning arrived; split it, so turned gives a word and up reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pin-ups are glamour models whose pictures are pinned to walls, so a kind of model.

clue.text: Floor was whiffy when rear wiped

indicators.note: wiping the rear clears away the back end, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: smelled bad, past tense of stink

explanation.surface: A floor smelled until someone's bottom was cleaned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor' reads as the ground underfoot; it is the verb meaning to knock flat or bewilder. Whiffy is British slang for smelly.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to knock them down or astonish them, just as to stun them is.

clue.text: Fitter lad crushed by big old player?

indicators.note: in a down entry, something crushed by another lies beneath it, so that piece comes after

blocks.note: OS is short for outsize, a clothing size for big
one who fits carpets
a son is a boy or lad

explanation.surface: A fitter young man is flattened by a hefty veteran sportsman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fitter' reads as healthier, but it is someone who fits carpets. 'Player' looks like sport; Oscar Peterson, who died in 2007, was a jazz pianist.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Peterson was a celebrated Canadian jazz pianist, a player of the piano from an earlier generation.

clue.text: Song and dance don't stop?

blocks.note: first meaning: a fuss or palaver
second meaning: an instruction to continue

explanation.walkthrough: A song and dance is an idiom for a needless fuss, not a performance.
explanation.definitionFit: A carry-on is British slang for a commotion or fuss, while carry on means keep going.

clue.text: On the podium if not after flipping, gymnastic star gets medal, finally

indicators.note: once flipped over, the words are read back to front
a gymnastic body twists and tumbles, so the letters are turned about
finally points to the last letter of the word before it

blocks.note: or means if not, as in 'hurry, or you'll be late'
the four letters rearranged
the final letter of medal

explanation.surface: A gymnast stands on the podium, flips, and wins a medal at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'If not after' looks like a contrast with being on the podium; it splits into 'if not', a word, and 'after flipping', which reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Rostral is the adjective from rostrum, a raised platform for speakers or medallists, so relating to the podium.

clue.text: Scrap approach

blocks.note: first meaning: a quarrel or brush with someone
second meaning: the final stretch leading up to something

explanation.walkthrough: Both words look like verbs, discard and come near, but each is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: A run-in is a minor argument, as with the police, and also the run-up or lead-in towards an event or finish.

clue.text: Westernmost city in Florida Panhandle, no place as far out

indicators.note: far out means wild or unconventional, so these letters are in a crazy order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A remote city at Florida's western tip is said to be like no other place so distant.
explanation.definitionFit: Pensacola is the city at the far western end of the Florida Panhandle, near the Alabama border.
